tasks.title: Define Human Entity Interface
tasks.description: Create the core TypeScript interface for a Human entity with all required properties for the first stage.
tasks.details: Create a new file `shared/types.ts` (or similar) to define the `Human` interface. This interface must include: `id: string`, `name: string`, `cityId: string`, `x: number`, `y: number`, `hunger: number` (0-100), `energy: number` (0-100), `currentAction: string` (e.g., 'idle', 'moving', 'eating', 'resting'). Also define a `HumanState` type if needed for WebSocket payloads. Ensure this type is shared between server and client.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify the interface compiles correctly in TypeScript. Manually check that all required fields are present and correctly typed.

tasks.title: Update City Interface to Reference Humans
tasks.description: Modify the existing City interface to include a list of human IDs instead of just a population count.
tasks.details: In `shared/types.ts`, update the `City` interface. Remove the `population: number` field. Add a new field `humanIds: string[]` which will store the IDs of humans residing in this city. Ensure backward compatibility is not required as this is a foundational change.
tasks.testStrategy: Confirm the updated City interface compiles and that existing code referencing `population` is flagged for update (expected).

tasks.title: Update World Interface to Include Humans
tasks.description: Extend the main World interface to include a collection of Human entities.
tasks.details: In `shared/types.ts`, update the `World` interface to include a `humans: Record<string, Human>` field. This allows O(1) lookup of any human by their ID. Ensure the existing `cities: Record<string, City>` field remains.
tasks.testStrategy: Verify the World interface includes both cities and humans, and compiles without errors.

tasks.title: Create Human Generator Utility
tasks.description: Implement a utility function to generate initial Human entities for existing cities.
tasks.details: Create a new file `server/humanGenerator.ts`. Implement a function `generateHumansForCity(city: City, count: number): Human[]` that creates `count` Human objects. Each human should have: a unique ID (e.g., using `uuid` or a simple counter), a randomly generated name (use a simple array of first/last names), the `cityId` set to the city's ID, initial `x` and `y` coordinates set to the city's location (or nearby), `hunger` and `energy` initialized to random values between 70-100, and `currentAction` set to 'idle'.
tasks.testStrategy: Write a small test script or manually invoke the function to ensure it returns the correct number of humans with valid properties and unique IDs.

tasks.title: Integrate Human Generation into World Initialization
tasks.description: Modify the world initialization logic to populate cities with Human entities during world creation.
tasks.details: In `server/worldStore.ts` (or wherever the initial world is created), after cities are generated, loop through each city and call `generateHumansForCity` with a reasonable starting population (e.g., 5-10 humans per city). Add the generated humans to the `world.humans` object and update each city's `humanIds` array with the new human IDs. Remove any logic that sets `city.population`.
tasks.testStrategy: Start the server and inspect the initial world state (e.g., via console log or WebSocket message) to confirm humans are created and linked to cities.

tasks.title: Update Simulation Engine to Process Humans Daily
tasks.description: Modify the simulation engine to update each Human's state every game day.
tasks.details: In `server/simulationEngine.ts`, within the main simulation tick (daily update), iterate over all humans in `world.humans`. For each human, implement basic daily updates: decrease `hunger` by 5-10 points, decrease `energy` by 3-7 points. Clamp values between 0 and 100. If `hunger` drops below 20, set `currentAction` to 'eating'. If `energy` drops below 20, set `currentAction` to 'resting'. Otherwise, set `currentAction` to 'idle' or 'moving' based on movement logic (see next task).
tasks.testStrategy: Run the simulation for several ticks and log human states to verify hunger/energy decrease and action changes occur correctly.

subtasks.title: Add human iteration loop to simulation tick
subtasks.description: In server/simulationEngine.ts, add a loop within the main simulation tick that iterates over all humans in world.humans.
subtasks.details: Locate the main simulation tick function in server/simulationEngine.ts. Add a for...in loop or Object.values() iteration over world.humans to process each human entity daily.

subtasks.title: Implement hunger and energy decrease logic
subtasks.description: For each human, decrease hunger by 5-10 points and energy by 3-7 points using random values within those ranges.
subtasks.details: Inside the human iteration loop, generate random decreases: hunger -= Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 5; energy -= Math.floor(Math.random() * 5) + 3;

subtasks.title: Add value clamping between 0 and 100
subtasks.description: Ensure hunger and energy values stay within valid range by clamping them between 0 and 100 after decreases.
subtasks.details: After decreasing values, apply clamping: human.hunger = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, human.hunger)); human.energy = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, human.energy));

subtasks.title: Implement action setting based on thresholds
subtasks.description: Set currentAction to 'eating' if hunger < 20, 'resting' if energy < 20, otherwise 'idle'.
subtasks.details: Add conditional logic after clamping: if (human.hunger < 20) human.currentAction = 'eating'; else if (human.energy < 20) human.currentAction = 'resting'; else human.currentAction = 'idle';

subtasks.title: Add logging for human state changes
subtasks.description: Add console logging to track human state changes during simulation ticks for debugging purposes.
subtasks.details: Add console.log statements to output human ID, hunger, energy, and currentAction after updates to verify the simulation is working correctly.

subtasks.title: Test simulation with multiple ticks
subtasks.description: Run the simulation for several ticks and verify that hunger/energy decrease and action changes occur correctly.
subtasks.details: Execute the simulation for 5-10 ticks and check console logs to ensure humans' hunger and energy are decreasing properly and actions are being set according to thresholds.
subtasks.testStrategy: Run simulation for multiple ticks and verify logged human states show correct hunger/energy decreases and appropriate action changes.

tasks.title: Implement Basic Random Movement for Humans
tasks.description: Add logic to allow humans to randomly move on the map each day.
tasks.details: In `server/simulationEngine.ts`, within the human update loop, add a movement step. If the human's action is not 'eating' or 'resting', there is a 30% chance the human will move. When moving, randomly adjust `x` and `y` by -1, 0, or +1, clamping to map boundaries (0-99 for 100x100 map). Set `currentAction` to 'moving' when movement occurs. Ensure movement is deterministic given a seed if needed, but simple Math.random() is acceptable for now.
tasks.testStrategy: Observe human coordinates over multiple ticks to confirm they change randomly and stay within bounds.

tasks.title: Update WebSocket World State Payload
tasks.description: Modify the WebSocket message to include the full human state alongside the world state.
tasks.details: In `server/socketHandler.ts`, when sending the world state to clients (e.g., on connection or on simulation tick), ensure the payload includes the `humans` object from the world. The message should be a JSON object like `{ type: 'worldState', data: { cities: {...}, humans: {...} } }`. Remove any population-only data from cities in the payload.
tasks.testStrategy: Connect a WebSocket client (e.g., browser console) and verify the received world state contains human data with correct structure.

tasks.title: Update Client to Receive and Store Humans
tasks.description: Modify the client-side state management to accept and store the humans data from WebSocket.
tasks.details: In the client code (likely in a context or state manager, e.g., `client/worldState.ts` or within `WorldView.tsx`), update the state to include a `humans: Record<string, Human>` field. When a `worldState` message is received from WebSocket, parse and store the `humans` data alongside `cities`. Ensure the Human type is imported from the shared types.
tasks.testStrategy: Log the client-side state after receiving a world state message to confirm humans are stored correctly.

tasks.title: Render Humans on the Map
tasks.description: Update the map renderer to display Human entities as visual elements on the map.
tasks.details: In `MapRenderer.tsx`, after rendering cities, iterate over the `humans` object. For each human, render a small colored dot (e.g., blue circle) at their `(x, y)` tile position. Use a distinct visual style from cities. Ensure the rendering is efficient (e.g., avoid re-rendering all humans unnecessarily, though optimization is not a priority yet).
tasks.testStrategy: Load the game and visually confirm that humans appear as dots on the map at their correct positions.

subtasks.title: Add human rendering logic to MapRenderer.tsx
subtasks.description: In MapRenderer.tsx, after the city rendering loop, add a new loop that iterates over the humans object and renders each human as a small blue circle at their (x, y) tile coordinates.
subtasks.details: After the existing city rendering code, add a forEach or Object.values(humans).map() loop. For each human, use ctx.beginPath(), ctx.arc(x, y, radius, 0, 2 * Math.PI), ctx.fillStyle = 'blue', ctx.fill(). Use tile size to convert (x, y) to pixel coordinates.
subtasks.testStrategy: Load the game and visually confirm that blue dots appear on the map at human positions.

subtasks.title: Define human dot styling constants
subtasks.description: Define styling constants for human dots (color, radius, stroke) to ensure visual distinction from cities.
subtasks.details: Add constants like HUMAN_DOT_RADIUS = 4, HUMAN_DOT_COLOR = '#3b82f6', HUMAN_DOT_STROKE = '#1e40af' at the top of MapRenderer.tsx. Apply these in the rendering loop for consistent styling.
subtasks.testStrategy: Verify that human dots have a distinct blue color and are smaller than city markers.

subtasks.title: Prepare click detection data structure
subtasks.description: Create a data structure to map pixel positions to human IDs for click detection.
subtasks.details: Create an array or Map called humanClickTargets that stores { id, x, y, radius } for each human. Populate this during the human rendering loop. This will be used in the click handler to determine which human was clicked.
subtasks.testStrategy: Log the humanClickTargets array to console and verify it contains correct positions and IDs.

subtasks.title: Implement onClick handler for human detection
subtasks.description: Add an onClick handler to the canvas that checks if a click intersects with any human dot.
subtasks.details: Add an onClick event to the canvas element. In the handler, calculate the click position relative to the canvas. Loop through humanClickTargets and check if the click is within radius + 5 pixels of any human. If found, call onHumanClick(humanId).
subtasks.testStrategy: Click on a human dot and verify the onHumanClick callback is invoked with the correct human ID.

subtasks.title: Add onHumanClick prop to MapRenderer
subtasks.description: Add an onHumanClick callback prop to MapRenderer component signature and wire it to the click handler.
subtasks.details: Update the MapRendererProps interface to include onHumanClick?: (humanId: string) => void. Pass this prop to the click detection logic. Ensure the component gracefully handles when the prop is not provided.
subtasks.testStrategy: Pass a mock onHumanClick function and verify it is called when clicking a human dot.

tasks.title: Enable Click Detection on Humans
tasks.description: Implement click event handling on the map to detect when a player clicks on a Human.
tasks.details: In `MapRenderer.tsx`, add an onClick handler to the human dot elements. When a human is clicked, trigger a callback (e.g., `onHumanClick(humanId: string)`) that is passed down from the parent component. Ensure the click target area is reasonable (e.g., 10x10 pixels around the dot).
tasks.testStrategy: Click on a human dot and verify the callback is invoked with the correct human ID.

tasks.title: Create Human Card Component
tasks.description: Build a UI component to display detailed information about a selected Human.
tasks.details: Create a new component `HumanCard.tsx`. This component should accept a `Human` object as a prop and display: name, current action, hunger level (as a progress bar or number), energy level (as a progress bar or number), and coordinates (x, y). Style it as a card or panel that can be overlaid on the map.
tasks.testStrategy: Render the HumanCard with sample data and verify all fields are displayed correctly.

tasks.title: Integrate Human Card into World View
tasks.description: Connect the HumanCard to the main view so it appears when a human is selected.
tasks.details: In `WorldView.tsx`, manage a `selectedHumanId` state. Pass the `onHumanClick` callback from Task 11 to `MapRenderer`. When a human is clicked, set `selectedHumanId`. Conditionally render the `HumanCard` component when `selectedHumanId` is not null, passing the corresponding human object from the state.
tasks.testStrategy: Click on a human and verify the HumanCard appears with the correct data. Click elsewhere and verify it disappears.

tasks.title: Implement Camera Follow for Selected Human
tasks.description: Add functionality to center the map camera on a selected human and follow them as they move.
tasks.details: In `WorldView.tsx` or `MapRenderer.tsx`, implement a camera system. When a human is selected, calculate the camera offset so the human is centered on the screen. On each world state update, if a human is selected, recalculate the camera position to keep them centered. Allow the player to pan the camera manually, but re-center when a new human is selected. Store camera state (offsetX, offsetY) in the component or context.
tasks.testStrategy: Select a human and verify the map centers on them. Move the camera manually, then select another human and verify it re-centers.

subtasks.title: Add camera state to WorldView component
subtasks.description: Introduce camera offset state (offsetX, offsetY) in WorldView.tsx or MapRenderer.tsx to track the current camera position.
subtasks.details: Add useState for cameraOffset: { x: number, y: number } initialized to { x: 0, y: 0 }. This will be used to translate the map rendering so the selected human stays centered.

subtasks.title: Implement camera centering calculation on human selection
subtasks.description: When a human is selected, compute the camera offset needed to center them on the screen.
subtasks.details: Create a function centerCameraOnHuman(human, canvasWidth, canvasHeight) that calculates offsetX = human.x - canvasWidth/2 and offsetY = human.y - canvasHeight/2. Call this function whenever a human is selected (from the onHumanClick callback).

subtasks.title: Apply camera offset to map rendering
subtasks.description: Modify the map rendering logic to apply the camera offset when drawing humans, cities, and other elements.
subtasks.details: In the canvas drawing logic, subtract cameraOffset.x from all x-coordinates and cameraOffset.y from all y-coordinates before rendering. This shifts the viewport so the camera follows the offset.

subtasks.title: Update camera position on world tick when human is selected
subtasks.description: On each world state update, if a human is selected, recalculate the camera offset to keep them centered.
subtasks.details: In the useEffect or update handler that processes new world state, check if a selectedHumanId exists. If so, find the human in the new state and call centerCameraOnHuman again to update the offset.

subtasks.title: Implement manual camera pan controls
subtasks.description: Allow the player to pan the camera by dragging or using arrow keys, updating the camera offset independently.
subtasks.details: Add mouse drag or keyboard event handlers that modify cameraOffset.x and cameraOffset.y. For drag: track mouse down, move, and up events to calculate delta. For keyboard: listen for arrow keys and adjust offset by a fixed step (e.g., 20px).

subtasks.title: Re-center camera when a new human is selected
subtasks.description: When the player selects a different human, override any manual pan and re-center the camera on the new selection.
subtasks.details: Ensure the onHumanClick handler always calls centerCameraOnHuman regardless of current manual pan state. This resets the offset to center on the newly selected human.

subtasks.title: Test camera follow and pan integration
subtasks.description: Verify that selecting a human centers the camera, the camera follows them on updates, manual pan works, and selecting a new human re-centers.
subtasks.details: Select a human and verify the map centers on them. Manually pan the camera away. Select a different human and verify the camera snaps to center on the new selection. Confirm the followed human stays centered as they move.
subtasks.testStrategy: Select a human and verify the map centers on them. Move the camera manually, then select another human and verify it re-centers.

tasks.title: Update Event Log to Show Human Actions
tasks.description: Enhance the EventLog component to display relevant human activities.
tasks.details: In `EventLog.tsx`, subscribe to simulation events or world state changes. When a human's action changes (e.g., from 'idle' to 'eating'), log a message like 'John Doe is eating'. Keep the log simple and limit the number of entries (e.g., last 50 events). Ensure events are timestamped or ordered.
tasks.testStrategy: Run the simulation and verify that human action changes appear in the event log.
